title: Why Platforms Flag Your IP: Proxy, VPN, and Tor Signals Explained
author: IP Ready
excerpt: A flag is not a ban. A teardown of the signals behind proxy, VPN, and Tor detections — and why stacking, not any single one, is what gets sessions blocked.
body:
Seeing Proxy: detected in a scan report is uncomfortable, but a flag is not a ban — it is one signal in a stack. Platforms rarely act on a single indicator. What gets sessions restricted is stacking: several signals that disagree with each other or with the story the session tells. Understanding each signal on its own is the first step to reading a report without panic.

The Signals That Fire

  • Proxy detection — the address belongs to infrastructure commonly used to forward traffic: hosting ranges, known relay services, or ports associated with proxies.
  • VPN endpoints — the IP appears on published lists of commercial VPN exit nodes. A VPN is a proxy with better marketing; platforms see it the same way.
  • Tor exits — traffic arriving from a public Tor exit relay. Anonymity is the point, so platforms treat every Tor session as untrusted.
  • Recent abuse — the address shows up in community-reported abuse databases, sometimes from a previous tenant of the same IP.
  • Location inconsistency — geography, timezone, and routing disagree, or the address has been seen in multiple countries recently.

What Stacking Means

Each signal alone has an innocent explanation. A VPN flag plus a datacenter ASN plus a timezone that does not match the registered country is no longer a set of coincidences — it is a pattern that looks like deliberate concealment. This is why one report row rarely matters while three adjacent rows can decide a session. When you read a scan, look for the story the signals tell together, not each line in isolation.

False Positives Happen

Plenty of flagged sessions are innocent. Corporate networks route thousands of employees through one NAT address, so one person's misbehavior stains everyone. Carrier-grade NAT puts entire mobile neighborhoods behind a single exit. Travel makes location look inconsistent even when the user is exactly where they say. If a flag does not match your setup, check whether you share the exit with others before assuming the report is about you.

The practical habit: scan before it matters, read the stack rather than the single flag, and change one variable at a time so you know what actually moved the result.
